title: Taiwan's reciprocal-trade commitments convert U.S. pressure into a planned capacity and procurement response
source_unit: U.S. Trade Representative fact sheet on the U.S.-Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade
geography: United States and Taiwan bilateral trade, semiconductor, energy, and strategic-technology relationship

observations.period: February 2026; announced U.S.-Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade

taiwan_tariff_action.value: Taiwan will eliminate or reduce 99 percent of tariff barriers and provide preferential access for named U.S. industrial and agricultural exports

taiwan_non_tariff_action.value: Taiwan committed to resolve or prevent named non-tariff barriers for U.S. vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and agricultural products

us_tariff_treatment.value: U.S. treatment of originating Taiwanese goods will apply the higher of the MFN rate or a 15 percent tariff rate, subject to stated exceptions

bilateral_trade_context.unit: US dollars billions; 2024 two-way goods and services trade, more than

observations.method: Bounded extraction from the official USTR fact sheet. Agreement terms are coded as a dated external-response and policy-implementation stage, not as observed trade-flow or firm-level outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The fact sheet does not establish legislative approval, implementation dates, realized tariff collections, export quantities, firm-level incidence, or whether the commitments changed Taiwanese or U.S. behavior relative to a counterfactual.
observations.subgroup: U.S. and Taiwanese governments, exporters, manufacturers, farmers, firms, and consumers; no individual firm or household is followed.
observations.counterinterpretation: An announced reciprocal framework can signal bargaining accommodation and market opening while later domestic formalities, exemptions, enforcement, or political change alter its practical effect.

observations.period: January 15, 2026 MOU referenced in the agreement fact sheet; planned Taiwan-linked U.S. capacity response

denominator.unit: AIT-TECRO memorandum and related industrial-park commitment

planned_us_industrial_parks.value: Taiwan side promises to work with the United States to establish industrial parks and industry clusters

planned_sector_scope.value: semiconductors supply chain, electronics manufacturing services including AI applications, energy, and other sectors

planned_taiwan_investment.value: Taiwan companies are expected to significantly increase investment in the United States, with financial support from Taiwan

section_232_treatment.value: U.S. preferential treatment for Taiwan was contemplated in semiconductor and semiconductor-equipment Section 232 measures, taking alignment and strategic partnership into account

observations.method: The USTR fact sheet's cross-reference to the AIT-TECRO MOU is kept separate from the existing Taiwan semiconductor record's investment and TSMC Arizona production observations. This is a planned bilateral-capacity response, not an independently audited output measure.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not provide project-level investors, disbursements, construction, production, ownership, workforce quality, energy or water burden, or measured reduction in Taiwan-centered supply dependence.
observations.subgroup: Taiwanese technology firms, U.S. semiconductor and energy firms, workers, host communities, and public agencies; project-level incidence is not observed.
observations.counterinterpretation: Partner investment can increase local resilience while leaving critical tools, materials, design, ownership, and operating knowledge externally concentrated; a policy promise is not replaceability.

observations.period: 2025–2029; planned Taiwanese purchases under the agreement

planned_lng_crude_purchases.unit: US dollars billions; planned LNG and crude-oil purchases

planned_aircraft_engine_purchases.unit: US dollars billions; planned civil aircraft and engine purchases

planned_power_and_equipment_purchases.unit: US dollars billions; planned power equipment, grids, materials, generators, storage, marine, steel-making, and other equipment

planned_total_named_purchases.unit: US dollars billions; arithmetic sum of three named plan categories, not independently reported total

realized_purchases.unit: missing delivery, payment, and trade-flow endpoint

observations.method: The three USTR-reported purchase categories are retained as planned bilateral-demand commitments. The combined figure is a transparent arithmetic sum and is not treated as realized U.S. exports or Taiwanese dependence.
observations.uncertainty: The fact sheet does not disclose contracts, delivery schedules by product, financing, counterparties, actual purchases, substitution, or whether the plan persists through 2029.
observations.subgroup: U.S. energy, aerospace, power-equipment, materials, and manufacturing sectors and Taiwanese public or private buyers; affected workers and households are not followed.
observations.counterinterpretation: A large purchasing plan can support U.S. sector demand and bargaining alignment without proving firm revenue, domestic job quality, household prices, or durable strategic leverage.

related_sources.claim: The prior Taiwan semiconductor record establishes a separate investment, first-fab production, workforce, and staged-expansion lane; this record adds the bilateral agreement and planned external-response layer.
The related USTR Section 301 notice supplies a separate trade-policy investigation context and is not pooled with this agreement-stage response.

boundary: This record establishes an announced Taiwan policy and market response to a U.S.-Taiwan reciprocal-trade framework, including planned U.S. capacity investment and purchases. It does not establish implementation, delivered output, firm or household incidence, supply-chain replacement, Taiwanese dependence, changed external behavior beyond the agreement commitments, or U.S. geopolitical leverage.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: USTR fact-sheet HTML retrieved and retained temporarily for extraction
